questions.q: Why must you put a resistor voltage divider on the HC-SR04's ECHO pin before connecting it to the Pi?
choices: To make the sensor measure longer distances
Because ECHO outputs 5 V, which would damage the Pi's 3.3 V GPIO pin
To limit the current so the sensor doesn't burn out
Because the Pi's GPIO pins are 5 V-tolerant and need the extra voltage
questions.explain: The HC-SR04's ECHO pin sends out a 5 V signal, but Pi 5 GPIO pins are 3.3 V only and not 5 V-tolerant. Without a divider, the 5 V can permanently destroy the pin — there is no fuse to protect it.

questions.q: Using the divider formula Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) with R1 = 330 Ω and R2 = 470 Ω on a 5 V ECHO signal, what voltage reaches the GPIO pin?
questions.explain: Vout = 5 × 470 ÷ (330 + 470) = 5 × 470 ÷ 800 = 2.94 V. That is safely below the 3.3 V limit yet still high enough for the Pi to read as a clear HIGH.

questions.q: Does the HC-SR04's TRIG pin also need a voltage divider?
choices: Yes, both TRIG and ECHO carry 5 V and need dividers
No — the Pi sends 3.3 V out to TRIG, which the sensor reads fine, so no divider is needed
Yes, because TRIG draws too much current
No, because TRIG is connected to a 5 V power pin
questions.explain: TRIG is an input to the sensor: the Pi drives it with 3.3 V out, which the HC-SR04 accepts happily. Only ECHO (sensor output, 5 V) endangers the Pi, so only ECHO needs the divider.

questions.q: In the line 'led = LED(17)', what are LED and led, in object-oriented terms?
choices: LED is the object and led is the class
Both are functions that return None
LED is the class (blueprint); led is an object built from it
LED is an attribute and led is a method
questions.explain: A class is a blueprint and an object is a real thing made from it. LED is the class; led is one specific object representing the LED on pin 17, with its own methods like led.on().

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'return' keyword in a function like read_distance_cm()?
choices: It prints the value to the screen and then forgets it
It hands a value back to the caller so it can be stored, tested, or reused
It restarts the function from the top
It deletes the function from memory
questions.explain: return passes a value back into the program. Unlike print(), which only displays text, a returned value can be captured in a variable, compared in an if statement, or passed to another function.
